questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This diagram shows the great vessels of the neck. Why does the right common carotid artery arise differently from the left?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both arise directly from the ascending aorta before the arch

choices.label: B
choices.text: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, whereas the left branches directly off the aortic arch

choices.label: C
choices.text: The right arises from the subclavian and the left from the pulmonary trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: The right arises from the aortic arch and the left from the vertebral artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Both arise from the brachiocephalic trunk but on opposite sides

explanation.summary: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so only the right common carotid is a second-order branch.
explanation.whyCorrect: The aortic arch gives off the brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid, and left subclavian. The brachiocephalic trunk then splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian, so only the right common carotid is a second-order branch.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This figure shows the arterial anastomoses of the nasal septum, including the anterior plexus outlined at the front. What common clinical event is this anterior region most associated with?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recurrent sinus infections

choices.label: B
choices.text: Referred pain to the ear

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anterior nosebleeds (epistaxis)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstructive sleep apnea

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the sense of smell

explanation.summary: The anterior septal anastomosis (Kiesselbach plexus) is a superficial convergence of several arteries and is the site of roughly 90% of nosebleeds. The posterior Woodruff plexus accounts for less common but heavier posterior bleeds.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anterior septal anastomosis (Kiesselbach plexus) is a superficial convergence of several arteries and is the site of roughly 90% of nosebleeds. The posterior Woodruff plexus accounts for less common but heavier posterior bleeds.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The paranasal sinuses are shown draining into the nasal cavity. Which of these sinuses is the largest and most frequently involved in sinusitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ethmoid air cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mastoid air cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sphenoid sinus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maxillary sinus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Frontal sinus

explanation.summary: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. Because their ostium sits high on the medial wall, gravity-dependent drainage is poor, making them the most commonly infected sinus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The maxillary sinuses are the largest paranasal sinuses. Because their ostium sits high on the medial wall, gravity-dependent drainage is poor, making them the most commonly infected sinus.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this open-mouth view, the paired masses seen on either side of the throat (between the palatine arches) are lymphoid tissue. What is their immunological role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are cartilage plates that keep the pharynx open

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are taste-bud clusters that detect bitter compounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are palatine tonsils that sample inhaled and ingested antigens as part of Waldeyer's ring

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are muscles that close the airway during swallowing

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are salivary glands that secrete digestive enzymes

explanation.summary: The palatine tonsils are aggregates of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue forming part of Waldeyer's ring. They trap pathogens entering via the mouth and nose and mount local immune responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The palatine tonsils are aggregates of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue forming part of Waldeyer's ring. They trap pathogens entering via the mouth and nose and mount local immune responses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This endoscopic photograph shows the laryngeal inlet during laryngoscopy. The paired mobile structures at the posterior ends of the vocal cords are functionally important because they do what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rotate and pivot to abduct and adduct the vocal cords

choices.label: B
choices.text: Filter particulate matter from inspired air

choices.label: C
choices.text: Secrete surfactant into the airway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sense blood oxygen tension

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This coronal section through the facial skeleton shows several air-filled, mucosa-lined cavities embedded within the frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, and maxillary bones. What is the primary functional role of these paired cavities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They lighten the skull and help warm and humidify inspired air

choices.label: B
choices.text: They provide the bony attachment for the extraocular muscles

choices.label: C
choices.text: They produce and secrete tears that drain to the eye

choices.label: D
choices.text: They house the primary olfactory receptor neurons

choices.label: E
choices.text: They generate cerebrospinal fluid for the anterior cranial fossa

explanation.summary: The cavities shown are the paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary). They reduce skull weight, add resonance to the voice, and their mucosa helps condition (warm/humidify) inspired air. Olfaction occurs at the cribriform plate, and tear production is a lacrimal-gland function.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cavities shown are the paranasal sinuses (frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary). They reduce skull weight, add resonance to the voice, and their mucosa helps condition (warm/humidify) inspired air. Olfaction occurs at the cribriform plate, and tear production is a lacrimal-gland function.

questions.imageRef: repic-035_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p7_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This coronal view of the nasal cavity highlights three paired, scroll-like bony projections along the lateral wall (color-coded) with air passages beneath each. What is the chief physiologic purpose of these projections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They anchor the vocal cords during phonation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They serve as the primary site of gas exchange

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contain the sensory endings for the gag reflex

choices.label: D
choices.text: They form the bony support of the hard palate

choices.label: E
choices.text: They increase mucosal surface area to warm, humidify, and filter inspired air

explanation.summary: The projections are the nasal conchae (turbinates). By creating turbulent airflow over a large mucosal surface, they warm, humidify, and filter inspired air. The spaces beneath them are the meatuses, into which sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct drain.
explanation.whyCorrect: The projections are the nasal conchae (turbinates). By creating turbulent airflow over a large mucosal surface, they warm, humidify, and filter inspired air. The spaces beneath them are the meatuses, into which sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct drain.

questions.imageRef: repic-036_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p8_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sagittal view of the lateral nasal wall shows the openings of the paranasal sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct into the nasal passages. What clinical phenomenon is explained by the drainage pathway of the nasolacrimal duct shown here?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of smell when the frontal sinus is blocked

choices.label: B
choices.text: Referred ear pain during swallowing

choices.label: C
choices.text: A runny nose when crying, because tears drain into the nasal cavity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hoarseness caused by postnasal drip onto the vocal cords

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nosebleeds arising from the sphenoid sinus

explanation.summary: The nasolacrimal duct drains lacrimal fluid from the medial canthus of the eye into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity. This is why excess tears (crying) produce a runny nose. Most paranasal sinuses drain into the middle meatus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The nasolacrimal duct drains lacrimal fluid from the medial canthus of the eye into the inferior meatus of the nasal cavity. This is why excess tears (crying) produce a runny nose. Most paranasal sinuses drain into the middle meatus.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: The larynx is divided into the three regions shown. Cancers arising in the middle region tend to present early and carry a relatively good prognosis because that region has which feature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ciliated pseudostratified epithelium

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct venous drainage into the portal system

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sparse lymphatic drainage

choices.label: D
choices.text: A dual arterial blood supply

choices.label: E
choices.text: The richest lymphatic drainage of the three

explanation.summary: The glottis (true cords) has minimal lymphatic drainage, so glottic carcinomas metastasize late and cause early hoarseness, giving them a better prognosis than the richly drained supraglottic and subglottic regions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The glottis (true cords) has minimal lymphatic drainage, so glottic carcinomas metastasize late and cause early hoarseness, giving them a better prognosis than the richly drained supraglottic and subglottic regions.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sagittal section shows the superior, middle, and inferior turbinates projecting into the nasal cavity. What is their main physiological role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They vibrate to produce the sound of the voice

choices.label: B
choices.text: They act as the primary site of oxygen absorption

choices.label: C
choices.text: They generate the pressure gradient that drives airflow

choices.label: D
choices.text: They house the cells that produce pulmonary surfactant

choices.label: E
choices.text: They increase mucosal surface area to warm, humidify, and filter inhaled air

explanation.summary: The turbinates (conchae) create turbulent airflow over a large mucosal surface, conditioning inspired air by warming, humidifying, and trapping particles before it reaches the lower airway.

questions.imageRef: repic-621_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p19_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this lateral view, structure 16 marks the carotid bifurcation with its associated carotid body. What is the primary function of the carotid body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a venous sinus that drains cerebral blood

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a peripheral chemoreceptor that senses arterial oxygen, CO2, and pH

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a lymph node filtering head and neck lymph

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes hormones that regulate calcium levels

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a baroreceptor that senses arterial blood pressure

explanation.summary: The carotid body at the bifurcation is a peripheral chemoreceptor. Falling PaO2 (or rising CO2 / falling pH) triggers it to increase ventilation via the glossopharyngeal nerve. The nearby carotid sinus is the baroreceptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The carotid body at the bifurcation is a peripheral chemoreceptor. Falling PaO2 (or rising CO2 / falling pH) triggers it to increase ventilation via the glossopharyngeal nerve. The nearby carotid sinus is the baroreceptor.

questions.imageRef: repic-622_Brick Exchange - Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract_p20_1.png

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In this midsagittal section, the leaf-shaped structure at the base of the tongue performs which protective action during swallowing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vibrates to produce voiced sound

choices.label: B
choices.text: Folds down over the laryngeal inlet to divert food into the esophagus and prevent aspiration

choices.label: C

explanation.whyCorrect: The epiglottis is a flap of elastic cartilage that folds posteriorly over the laryngeal aditus during deglutition, directing the bolus into the esophagus and protecting the airway from aspiration.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This is the view of the larynx seen during laryngoscopy. The paired pale white folds are the true vocal cords, which appear whiter than the surrounding mucosa mainly because they are what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Relatively avascular, covered by stratified squamous epithelium over the vocal ligament

choices.label: B
choices.text: Densely packed with blood-filled sinusoids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coated with a thick layer of mucus

explanation.whyCorrect: The true vocal folds have little blood supply and are covered by stratified squamous epithelium over the dense vocal ligament, so they appear pearly white compared with the well-vascularized false (vestibular) folds above them.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This endoscopic image captures the vocal folds during phonation. Sound is produced when what happens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expired air passes through the adducted cords, causing them to vibrate

choices.label: B
choices.text: The epiglottis vibrates against the tongue base

choices.label: C

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: In these posterior and lateral views of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, one highlighted muscle is unique among them all. What is that unique function?

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This lateral dissection of the larynx highlights an intrinsic muscle running from the cricoid to the arytenoid on the side of the larynx. Its primary action is to do what?

choices.label: A

questions.stem: This dissection shows the infrahyoid (strap) muscles. Their principal collective action is what?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depress the hyoid bone and larynx after they have been elevated

questions.stem: This figure color-codes the extrinsic muscles of the tongue. Which of these muscles protrudes the tongue, so that when it is paralyzed on one side the protruded tongue deviates toward the affected side?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Geniohyoid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Styloglossus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Genioglossus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyoglossus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Palatoglossus

explanation.summary: Genioglossus protrudes the tongue; with a unilateral hypoglossal (CN XII) lesion the intact side pushes across the midline, so the tongue deviates toward the weak side on protrusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Genioglossus protrudes the tongue; with a unilateral hypoglossal (CN XII) lesion the intact side pushes across the midline, so the tongue deviates toward the weak side on protrusion.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This figure shows the nerve supply of the larynx. Injury to the nerve looping below the larynx (for example during thyroid surgery) most characteristically produces what?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anesthesia of the facial skin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete loss of smell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hoarseness from vocal cord paralysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inability to elevate the soft palate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of taste on the anterior tongue

explanation.summary: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid; injury (a risk in thyroid surgery, where it runs near the inferior thyroid artery) causes vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid; injury (a risk in thyroid surgery, where it runs near the inferior thyroid artery) causes vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness.

questions.topicName: Anatomy of the Upper Respiratory Tract
questions.stem: This sagittal view divides the nasal cavity into functional regions. The small region highlighted orange at the roof of the cavity is responsible for which function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Detection of smell (olfaction)

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drainage of tears into the nose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Warming and humidifying air

choices.label: D
choices.text: Production of voiced sound

choices.label: E
choices.text: Equalization of middle-ear pressure

explanation.summary: The olfactory region at the roof of the nasal cavity is lined by specialized olfactory epithelium containing bipolar sensory neurons that detect odorants; the larger respiratory region conditions inspired air.
explanation.whyCorrect: The olfactory region at the roof of the nasal cavity is lined by specialized olfactory epithelium containing bipolar sensory neurons that detect odorants; the larger respiratory region conditions inspired air.
